title: Ang 146–150: Majh ki Var ends
tomorrow: what's heavier than anything you've ever lifted?

cards: A building can look holy from the street: a dome, wide steps, a sign out front. What happens inside a person is harder to photograph. So what would a mosque built out of mercy look like?
As Majh ki Var heads for its last pauris, ang 146 to 150, it has already asked that question, a few pages back, and answered it with respect for its Muslim neighbors.

teach.b: The question underneath: what makes someone truly religious?

teach.h: MERCY YOUR MOSQUE, TRUTH YOUR GUIDE.
teach.b: On ang 140, Guru Nanak speaks to Muslims, in paraphrase: make mercy your mosque, faith your prayer mat, honest earning your Qur'an. Make modesty and good conduct your observance and your fast; so be a Muslim.
Let good deeds be your Kaaba and truth your guide. And on ang 141: it's hard to be called a Muslim; whoever truly is one, let them be called a Muslim. He isn't mocking the mosque.
He holds up the Muslim ideal and asks for it lived all the way through. Now the neighbor, in its own words.
The Qur'an, surah 2, verse 177, says, in paraphrase: righteousness isn't turning your face to the east or the west.

The righteous believe in God and the Last Day, the angels, the Scripture and the prophets; give wealth, out of love for Him, to relatives, orphans, the needy and the traveler; keep the prayer; keep their promises; and stay patient in hardship.

The shared ground: the outward form points past itself to a life, and the life is the measure. The honest difference: in that verse, the prayer stays, alongside belief in angels, Scripture and prophets.
Muslims keep it. Guru Nanak's salok turns mosque, mat and fast into virtues, and Sikhs keep their own forms: the gurdwara, the Granth, the daily prayers.
Then the ballad's closing pauris finish its praise of the One, and the var is done.

how: Sikhs reading in order finish Majh ki Var on ang 150 before the raga Gauri begins; the ang 140 salok, mercy your mosque, is quoted in Sikh talks on what makes faith real.

games.q: a mosque of mercy — tap the pairs.
p: righteousness isn't facing east or west

s: Guru Nanak told Muslims to stop going to the mosque
he held up the Muslim ideal and asked for it lived: mercy as the mosque, truth as the guide.
Qur'an 2:177 says righteousness isn't turning your face to east or west
it names belief, giving to those in need, keeping prayer and promises, and patience.
the salok and the Qur'an verse say the same thing in every way
both measure faith by the life; in the verse the prayer stays, and Sikhs keep their own forms.

games.q: two friends at lunch, one Muslim, one Sikh, argue about whether outward practice matters at all. you've read ang 140 and Qur'an 2:177. what's fair to both?
o: both texts say forms are useless and should be dropped.
both measure faith by the life; each tradition keeps its own forms.
they teach exactly the same thing, so the argument is pointless.
games.why: shared measure: the life. honest difference: the verse keeps the prayer as part of righteousness; the salok turns the forms into virtues, and Sikhs keep their own.

practice: If you can, read the last pauri on ang 150 first. Then listen for one sound near you, a voice in another room, traffic, a bird, and let it stand for a neighbor whose prayers sound different from yours.
Hold that sound kindly until it fades.
